title: Chapter 26
paragraphs: The outward relations of Alexey Alexandrovitch and his wife had not changed. The only difference was that he was busier than ever. As in earlier years, he had gone abroad at the start of spring to a foreign watering place for the sake of his health, which was strained each year by the winter's work that grew heavier and heavier. And, as always, he returned in July and at once threw himself into work with even greater energy. As usual, too, his wife had moved out of town for the summer to a villa, while he remained in Petersburg. From the date of their conversation after the party at Princess Tverskaya's he had never again spoken to Anna of his suspicions and jealousy, and that habitual tone of mocking mimicry was the most convenient possible for his present attitude toward his wife. He was a little colder to her. He seemed merely a little put out with her over that first midnight conversation, which she had brushed aside. In his manner toward her there was a shade of vexation, but nothing more. "You wouldn't be open with me," he seemed to be telling her in his mind; "so much the worse for you. Now you may beg as much as you like, but I will not be open with you. So much the worse for you!" he said inwardly, like a man who, having vainly tried to put out a fire, flies into a rage at his own useless efforts and says, "Oh, very well then — you can burn for this!" This man, so subtle and shrewd in official life, did not realize all the senselessness of such an attitude toward his wife. He did not realize it because it was too terrible for him to grasp his real position, and he had shut down and locked and sealed up in his heart that secret place where his feelings about his family — that is, his wife and son — lay hidden. He, who had been such a careful father, had grown peculiarly cold to his son from the end of that winter on, and adopted toward him the same bantering tone he used with his wife. "Aha, young man!" was the greeting with which he met him.

Alexey Alexandrovitch asserted, and believed, that he had never in any previous year had so much official business as that year. But he was not aware that he was seeking out work for himself that year — that this was one of the means of keeping shut that secret place where his feelings about his wife and son and his thoughts about them lay hidden, growing more terrible the longer they lay there. If anyone had had the right to ask Alexey Alexandrovitch what he thought of his wife's behavior, the mild and peaceable Alexey Alexandrovitch would have given no answer, but he would have been deeply angered with anyone who put the question to him. For this reason there came into Alexey Alexandrovitch's face a look of haughtiness and severity whenever anyone inquired after his wife's health. Alexey Alexandrovitch did not want to think at all about his wife's behavior, and he actually succeeded in not thinking about it at all.

Alexey Alexandrovitch's permanent summer villa was in Peterhof, and Countess Lidia Ivanovna usually spent the summer there, close to Anna, and constantly in her company. That year Countess Lidia Ivanovna declined to settle in Peterhof, did not come to see Anna Arkadyevna once, and, in conversation with Alexey Alexandrovitch, hinted at the unsuitability of Anna's close intimacy with Betsy and Vronsky. Alexey Alexandrovitch cut her short sharply, declaring outright that his wife was above suspicion, and from that time on he began to avoid Countess Lidia Ivanovna. He did not want to see, and did not see, that many people in society cast dubious glances at his wife; he did not want to understand, and did not understand, why his wife had so particularly insisted on staying at Tsarskoe, where Betsy was staying, and not far from the camp of Vronsky's regiment. He did not allow himself to think about it, and he did not think about it; and yet, although he never admitted it to himself and had no proofs, not even circumstantial ones, in the bottom of his heart he knew beyond all doubt that he was a deceived husband, and he was profoundly miserable about it.

How often during those eight years of happy life with his wife had Alexey Alexandrovitch looked at other men's unfaithful wives and other deceived husbands and asked himself: "How can people sink to that? How is it they don't put an end to such a hideous position?" But now, when the misfortune had come upon himself, he was so far from thinking of putting an end to the position that he refused to acknowledge it at all — refused precisely because it was too awful, too unnatural.

Since his return from abroad Alexey Alexandrovitch had been at their country villa twice. Once he dined there, and another time he spent the evening there with a party of friends, but he had not once stayed the night there, as had been his habit in previous years.

The day of the races was a very busy one for Alexey Alexandrovitch; but when he was mentally planning out the day that morning, he had decided to go to their country house to see his wife immediately after dinner, and from there to the races, which the whole court would be attending and at which he was obliged to be present. He was going to see his wife because he had made up his mind to see her once a week to keep up appearances. And besides, on that day, being the fifteenth, he had to give his wife some money for her expenses, according to their usual arrangement.
With his habitual control over his thoughts, although he thought all this about his wife, he did not let his thoughts wander any further with regard to her.

That morning was a very full one for Alexey Alexandrovitch. The evening before, Countess Lidia Ivanovna had sent him a pamphlet by a celebrated traveler in China, who was staying in Petersburg, and with it a note begging him to see the traveler in person, as he was an extremely interesting man from various angles and likely to be of use. Alexey Alexandrovitch had not had time to read the pamphlet through in the evening, and finished it in the morning. Then people began arriving with petitions, and came the reports, the interviews, the appointments, the dismissals, the apportionment of rewards, pensions, grants, notes — the workaday round, as Alexey Alexandrovitch called it, that always ate up so much time. Then there was private business of his own — a visit from the doctor and from the steward who managed his property. The steward did not take long. He simply handed Alexey Alexandrovitch the money he needed along with a brief account of the state of his affairs, which was not altogether satisfactory, since it had happened that during that year, because of increased expenses, more had been paid out than usual, and there was a deficit. But the doctor, a celebrated Petersburg doctor who was an intimate acquaintance of Alexey Alexandrovitch's, took up a great deal of time. Alexey Alexandrovitch had not expected him that day, and was surprised at his visit, and even more so when the doctor questioned him very carefully about his health, listened to his breathing, and tapped at his liver. Alexey Alexandrovitch did not know that his friend Lidia Ivanovna, noticing that he was not as well as usual that year, had begged the doctor to go and examine him. "Do it for my sake," Countess Lidia Ivanovna had said to him.
"I will do it for the sake of Russia, countess," the doctor answered.
"A priceless man!" said Countess Lidia Ivanovna.

The doctor was extremely dissatisfied with Alexey Alexandrovitch. He found the liver considerably enlarged and the digestive powers weakened, while the course of mineral waters had been entirely without effect. He prescribed more physical exercise so far as possible, and as far as possible less mental strain, and above all no worry — in other words, just what was as much out of Alexey Alexandrovitch's power as abstaining from breathing. Then he withdrew, leaving Alexey Alexandrovitch with an uncomfortable sense that something was wrong with him, and that there was no chance of curing it.

As he was leaving, the doctor happened to meet on the staircase an acquaintance of his, Sludin, the secretary of Alexey Alexandrovitch's department. They had been comrades at the university, and though they rarely met, they thought highly of each other and were excellent friends, and so there was no one to whom the doctor would have given his opinion of a patient as freely as to Sludin.
"How glad I am you've been seeing him!" said Sludin. "He's not well, and I think.... Well, what's your verdict?"

"I'll tell you," said the doctor, beckoning over Sludin's head to his coachman to bring the carriage round. "It's like this," the doctor said, taking a finger of his kid glove in his white hands and pulling on it, "if you don't strain the strings and then try to break them, you'll find it a hard job; but strain a string to its very limit, and the mere weight of one finger on the strained string will snap it. And with his close attention to detail, his conscientious devotion to his work, he's strained to the limit; and there's some outside burden weighing on him, and not a light one," the doctor concluded, raising his eyebrows significantly. "Will you be at the races?" he added as he sank into his seat in the carriage.
"Yes, yes, of course; it does waste a lot of time," the doctor answered vaguely to some remark from Sludin he hadn't caught.

Right after the doctor, who had taken up so much time, came the celebrated traveler, and Alexey Alexandrovitch, with the help of the pamphlet he had only just finished reading and his previous familiarity with the subject, impressed the traveler with the depth of his knowledge and the breadth and enlightenment of his view of it.

At the same time as the traveler, a provincial marshal of nobility on a visit to Petersburg was announced, and Alexey Alexandrovitch had to have some conversation with him. After his departure, Alexey Alexandrovitch had to finish the daily routine of business with his secretary, and then he still had to drive over to call on a certain great personage on a matter of grave and serious import. Alexey Alexandrovitch only just managed to be back by five o'clock, his dinner hour, and after dining with his secretary he invited him to drive with him to his country villa and to the races.
Though he did not admit it to himself, Alexey Alexandrovitch was now always trying to secure the presence of a third person in his meetings with his wife.
